newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians protest for second day, crowds grow.
newsitem.headline: Albanians protest for second day, crowds grow.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Albanians, blaming the government for the collapse of investment schemes, swept through lines of riot police on Thursday to occupy the city centre in a second day of protests.
An angry crowd of some 10,000, with women and children at the front and swelling by the hour, brushed aside a thin cordon of police in mid-morning to reach the main Independence Square.
Within hours, the numbers had swelled to 30,000 as residents of surrounding mountain villagers swarmed into the Adriatic port.

"Vlore is ours, down with the government!" the crowd chanted, demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha's right-wing government. "Sali, you thief, where have you put our money," others shouted back.
The marchers then moved on silently to the regional administrative offices.

The protests, sparked by the collapse of one scheme based in the area, engulfed the centre of the city throughout Wednesday. Police fought pitched battles with demonstrators, but twice failed to disperse them.
Some demonstrators ran to a city high school and persuaded pupils to leave classromms and join the gathering.
The interior ministry said three demonstrators and three policemen were injured in Wednesday's clashes during which security forces deployed water cannon and dogs and shots periodically rang out.

The official ATA news agency said police had arrested a number of "terrorists" after Wednesday's demonstration, the first in the Balkan country since angry depositors set fire to public buildings in several cities last month.
More than 150 people were arrested after those disturbances and prosecutors pledged to seek minimum 15-year jail terms.
Virtually every family has invested money in the schemes in the six years since Albania has emerged from eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime.
Partial refunds are being dispensed for two failed pyramid schemes but many depositors are angry that they are not getting their entire stake back.
Some accuse the ruling Democratic Party, founded by Berisha, of using the proceeds to finance its re-election in polls last year, denounced as rigged by Western observers.

Gjallica, based in Vlore, owed depositors an estimated $500 million and was the fifth major pyramid scheme to go bankrupt since November. A small number of other investment schemes are clinging to life, although they have cut interest payments.
Local economists believe as much as $2 billion was tied up in all the schemes and say the collapse of other companies is inevitable and could pitch Albania into uncontrollable violence.
